title: 11 Things Vampire Teachers Do That Cause Stress And Drama
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Written as a deliberately pointed callout, Linsin describes teachers who make life harder for their colleagues through ego and drama-seeking, naming eleven specific behaviors that define this type: stealing or dismissing others' ideas, excessive complaining, gossiping, scolding students in front of a supervising colleague, dominating staff meetings, bragging, currying favor with the principal, hijacking meeting time with self-focused questions, conspiring to keep certain students out of their class, bullying other teachers, and throwing colleagues under the bus. He frames the piece as a response to hearing repeatedly from stressed-out colleagues of these 'vampire teachers,' and argues that even keeping your head down isn't always enough to escape their impact, and that speaking up can backfire. He invites readers to add to the list and share it with colleagues, framing the article as a small act of collective pushback against this pattern of behavior in schools.
points: Vampire teachers steal or dismiss colleagues' ideas, dominate staff meetings, and ask questions that only pertain to themselves.
A hallmark behavior is scolding students in front of the supervising teacher, a public power move at a colleague's expense.
They conspire to keep certain students out of their own class while insinuating themselves into the principal's inner circle.
They make themselves look good by throwing other teachers under the bus rather than taking responsibility.
Linsin acknowledges that simply keeping your head down isn't always enough to escape a vampire teacher's impact, and that speaking up can backfire.
quotes: Some teachers seem to revel in drama and making life harder for their colleagues. They love victimhood and high status.
They believe that they’re the greatest educator since Anne Sullivan, yet have no idea the destruction they cause to school climate and culture.
To join their midst is easy. It takes nothing more than a bad attitude and an insatiable ego to put yourself first.
Please forgive the negative slant of the article, but after hearing from dozens and dozens of their stressed-out colleagues over the years, I think it’s high time they’re called out.
Teaching is challenging enough all on its own. A single colleague can make the experience downright insufferable.
I hear from teachers every week seeking advice on how to handle these vampires who seem to go out of their way to cause stress and drama. Sometimes keeping your head down isn’t enough.
